_about: Curated additions and corrections merged over the generated dso.json at load time (src/catalog/dso.ts applyCuratedDSO). Never hand-edit dso.json: it is importer output. Added entries are taken from OpenNGC database_files/addendum.csv (rows named in each entry's source). Like dso.json, this file is derived from OpenNGC and is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0, not the Apache-2.0 code licence (see NOTICE).

add.name: LMC
add.description: A satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, about 160,000 light-years away. From the southern hemisphere it is an obvious naked-eye glow, like a detached piece of the Milky Way. It holds the Tarantula Nebula (NGC 2070), the most active star-forming region in the Local Group.
notableFeatures: Naked-eye galaxy from the southern hemisphere
Contains the Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus, NGC 2070)
add.imagingNotes: About 11° across: a wide-field lens, not a telescope, frames it whole.
add.source: OpenNGC addendum.csv row ESO056-115 (position, size, magnitudes, type). Distance 49.6 kpc: Pietrzyński et al. 2019, Nature 567, 200.

add.name: M45
add.description: The Seven Sisters: the brightest open cluster in the sky, a tight dipper of blue-white stars that the naked eye splits into six or seven. The faint blue haze in long exposures is a dust cloud the cluster happens to be passing through.
add.imagingNotes: About 2.5° across: a short refractor or a telephoto lens; the nebulosity needs dark skies and long integration.
add.source: OpenNGC addendum.csv row Mel022 (M=045). Distance from its parallax (7.364 mas).

add.name: M40
add.description: Not a nebula at all: a pair of unrelated 9th and 10th magnitude stars about 50 arcseconds apart that Charles Messier logged in 1764 while searching for a nebula reported in this part of Ursa Major.
notableFeatures: Optical double star, not a physical pair
add.source: OpenNGC addendum.csv row M040 (type **, V 8.0, WDS J12222+5805AB).

notableFeatures: OpenNGC (following NED) treats M102 as a duplicate observation of M101; many observers identify M102 with NGC 5866 instead
Often identified as M102 (OpenNGC notes "This may be M102")
Lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud
The most active star-forming region in the Local Group
